q: The Constitution is best described as:
choices: An ordinary statute that Congress may amend
The fundamental and supreme law, to which all laws, acts and treaties must conform
A guide with no binding force
hints: The people, not Congress, ordained it.
Any contrary law is void.
why: The Constitution is the supreme law, ordained by the sovereign people; a law, treaty or act contrary to it is void (doctrine of constitutional supremacy). The 1987 Constitution took effect upon its ratification on February 2, 1987.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Preamble and Art. XVIII, Sec. 27

q: Congress passed a law providing that it shall prevail over any inconsistent provision of the Constitution. Is the law valid?

alac.answer: No; the Constitution is the supreme law, and any law contrary to it is void.
alac.basis: The 1987 Constitution was ordained and promulgated by the sovereign Filipino people, as its Preamble declares. Under the doctrine of constitutional supremacy, the Constitution is the fundamental law to which all laws must conform; Congress, as a creation of the Constitution, cannot place its own acts above it.
alac.application: Here, the law claims to prevail over the Constitution itself.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the law is void.

cite: 1987 Constitution, Preamble and Art. XVIII, Sec. 27

q: Under Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS, provisions of the Constitution are presumed to be:
choices: Self-executing, unless the Constitution itself makes them dependent on legislation
hints: Presumption: self-executing.
Art. II principles are generally not.
why: Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS, G.R. No. 122156, February 3, 1997: constitutional provisions are presumed self-executing; the Filipino First policy (Art. XII, Sec. 10, par. 2) was enforced without an implementing law. Most of Art. II (state policies) are not self-executing, but some, like the right to a balanced and healthful ecology, are.
cite: Manila Prince Hotel v. Government Service Insurance System, G.R. No. 122156, February 3, 1997; 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 10

q: In the sale of a historic hotel, the GSIS chose a foreign bidder over a qualified Filipino corporation that matched the bid. The GSIS argued that the Filipino First provision needs a law before it can be enforced. Is the GSIS correct?

alac.answer: No; the provision is self-executing, and the Filipino bidder who matched the bid must be preferred.
alac.basis: Article XII, Section 10 of the 1987 Constitution provides that in the grant of rights, privileges, and concessions covering the national economy and patrimony, the State shall give preference to qualified Filipinos. In Manila Prince Hotel v. Government Service Insurance System, G.R. No. 122156, February 3, 1997, the Supreme Court held that constitutional provisions are presumed self-executing, and enforced this provision without an implementing law.
alac.application: Here, the hotel is part of the national patrimony, and a qualified Filipino matched the foreign bid.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the GSIS must award the sale to the Filipino bidder.

cite: Manila Prince Hotel v. Government Service Insurance System, G.R. No. 122156, February 3, 1997; 1987 Constitution, Art. XII, Sec. 10

q: Under Article XVII, a people's initiative may propose:
hints: Quantitative and qualitative tests for revision.
Initiative cannot revise.
why: Art. XVII: amendments or revisions may be proposed by Congress (three-fourths vote) or a constitutional convention; a people's initiative (12% of registered voters, at least 3% per district) may propose only amendments (Sec. 2). Lambino v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 174153, October 25, 2006: shifting from bicameral-presidential to unicameral-parliamentary is a revision, which initiative cannot propose; the petition must also show the full text to signatories.
cite: Lambino v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 174153, October 25, 2006; 1987 Constitution, Art. XVII, Secs. 1 and 2

q: A group gathered signatures of 15% of registered voters for a petition to abolish the Senate and replace the presidential system with a parliamentary one. May this be done by people's initiative?

alac.answer: No; the proposal is a revision, which cannot be proposed through people's initiative.
alac.basis: Article XVII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution allows the people to directly propose amendments through initiative upon a petition of at least twelve per centum of the total number of registered voters. In Lambino v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 174153, October 25, 2006, the Supreme Court held that a change from a bicameral-presidential to a unicameral-parliamentary system is a revision because it alters the basic plan of government, and revisions cannot be proposed by initiative.
alac.application: Here, the proposal would abolish the Senate and change the form of government.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, it must be proposed by Congress or a constitutional convention, not by initiative.

cite: Lambino v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 174153, October 25, 2006; 1987 Constitution, Art. XVII, Secs. 1 and 2

q: The elements of a State are:
hints: Recognition is not an element.
Government is the agent, not the State itself.
why: The four elements: people (a community large enough to be self-sufficient), territory (a fixed portion of the earth), government (the agency through which the will of the State is expressed) and sovereignty (supreme power, internal and external). Recognition by other States is not an element.
cite: Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States (1933), Art. 1

q: A group occupied an uninhabited island, set up officials and declared itself a new State, but no other country has recognized it. Is recognition by other States an element of statehood?

alac.answer: No; the elements are people, territory, government and sovereignty; recognition is not an element, although it affects the entity's relations with other States.
alac.basis: Under international law, reflected in Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention, a State as a person of international law has a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other States, which in Philippine doctrine is expressed as sovereignty.
alac.application: Here, the group's claim must be judged by whether it has these four elements, not by recognition. An uninhabited island occupied by a small group may lack a permanent population.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, lack of recognition does not by itself defeat statehood, but the entity must still prove all four elements.

cite: Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States (1933), Art. 1

q: Under Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution, sovereignty resides in:
choices: The people, from whom all government authority emanates
hints: Sovereignty belongs to the people.
Occupation suspends only the exercise of sovereignty.
why: Art. II, Sec. 1: the Philippines is a democratic and republican State; sovereignty resides in the people. Sovereignty is permanent, exclusive, comprehensive, absolute, indivisible, inalienable and imprescriptible; it is not suspended during enemy occupation (only its exercise is).

q: During a foreign military occupation, the occupant enacted rules for the occupied territory. After liberation, a party argued that Philippine sovereignty was lost during the occupation. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No; sovereignty is not lost by enemy occupation; only its exercise is suspended.
alac.basis: Article II, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution declares that sovereignty resides in the people and all government authority emanates from them. Under settled doctrine, sovereignty is permanent; during belligerent occupation, the sovereign's exercise of power is merely suspended, and it returns upon liberation (jus postliminium).
alac.application: Here, the occupation was temporary and ended with liberation.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Philippine sovereignty was never lost; only its exercise was suspended.

keyPoints: Sovereignty resides in the people (Art. II, Sec. 1)

q: Under the doctrine of state immunity, the State:
choices: May not be sued without its consent, which may be express (by law) or implied
Is immune only in criminal cases
hints: Suability is not liability.
Public funds are not subject to garnishment.
why: Art. XVI, Sec. 3: the State cannot be sued without its consent. Consent may be express (a general or special law) or implied (when the State enters into a business contract in its proprietary capacity, or files a suit). Consent to be sued is not consent to execution: public funds cannot be garnished without an appropriation (see PD 1445, Sec. 26).

q: A contractor won a money judgment against a government agency whose charter allows it to sue and be sued. The contractor sought to garnish the agency's funds in a government bank. May the funds be garnished?

alac.answer: As a rule, no; consent to be sued does not include consent to the execution of the judgment against public funds, which can be paid only pursuant to an appropriation by law.
alac.basis: Article XVI, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State may not be sued without its consent. The Supreme Court has held that suability does not mean liability, and that public funds cannot be the object of garnishment proceedings even if consent to be sued has been given, since their disbursement must be covered by an appropriation made by law.
alac.application: Here, the agency's charter allowed it to be sued, but the funds are public and no appropriation covers the judgment.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the contractor must file his claim with the Commission on Audit rather than garnish the funds.

keyPoints: Suability vs. liability; no garnishment of public funds

q: In Belgica v. Ochoa, the PDAF system was struck down partly because:
choices: It allowed legislators to take part in post-enactment acts of budget execution, violating separation of powers
It was passed by the Senate only
hints: Once a budget is enacted, execution belongs to the Executive.
Each branch is supreme in its own sphere.
why: Separation of powers: legislative power in Congress (Art. VI, Sec. 1), executive power in the President (Art. VII, Sec. 1), judicial power in the courts (Art. VIII, Sec. 1). Belgica v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 208566, November 19, 2013: legislators' post-enactment identification of projects (pork barrel) encroached on executive budget execution.
cite: Belgica v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 208566, November 19, 2013; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 1; Art. VII, Sec. 1; Art. VIII, Sec. 1

q: A new law allows each Senator, after the budget is passed, to choose which projects in his province will receive a lump-sum fund. Is the law valid?

alac.answer: No; it lets legislators take part in the execution of the budget, which violates separation of powers.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution vests legislative power in Congress, and Article VII, Section 1 vests executive power in the President. In Belgica v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 208566, November 19, 2013, the Supreme Court held that legislators' post-enactment participation in the identification of projects under a lump-sum fund is an unconstitutional encroachment on the executive's power to implement the budget.
alac.application: Here, Senators would choose projects after the budget is enacted.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the law violates the separation of powers.

keyPoints: Budget execution belongs to the Executive
cite: Belgica v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 208566, November 19, 2013; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 1; Art. VII, Sec. 1; Art. VIII, Sec. 1

q: Which is an example of checks and balances under the Constitution?
choices: The President's veto of a bill, which Congress may override by a two-thirds vote of each House
The President appointing his own Cabinet without limit
hints: Separation of powers is balanced by checks.
Examples: veto, override, judicial review, impeachment.
why: Checks and balances let each branch restrain the others: the presidential veto and congressional override (Art. VI, Sec. 27), Senate concurrence in treaties, Commission on Appointments confirmation, judicial review, impeachment, and the power of the purse.

q: The President vetoed a bill. Two-thirds of the House voted to override, but only half of the Senators did. Did the bill become a law?

alac.answer: No; an override requires two-thirds of all the Members of each House.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 27 of the 1987 Constitution provides that every bill passed by Congress shall, before it becomes a law, be presented to the President, who may veto it; the bill becomes a law only if, upon reconsideration, two-thirds of all the Members of each House agree to pass it. This is a check by the Executive on Congress, balanced by Congress's power to override.
alac.application: Here, the Senate did not reach two-thirds.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the veto stands and the bill did not become a law.

keyPoints: Two-thirds of all Members of each House

q: For a valid delegation of legislative power to an administrative agency, the law must:
choices: Simply say the agency may make rules
Be complete in itself and fix a sufficient standard to guide the delegate
Be approved by the Supreme Court first
Be passed by a two-thirds vote
hints: Completeness test and sufficient standard test.
Congress cannot be stripped of its oversight by legislative veto.
why: Delegated power cannot be further delegated (potestas delegata non delegari potest), but permissible delegations include tariff powers to the President, emergency powers, delegation to the people, to local governments, and to administrative bodies; the tests are completeness and sufficient standard (ABAKADA Guro Party List v. Purisima, G.R. No. 166715, August 14, 2008).
cite: ABAKADA Guro Party List v. Purisima, G.R. No. 166715, August 14, 2008; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 1

q: A law allows a new agency to impose "such regulations as it deems wise" on any business, with no stated policy or limits. Is the delegation valid?

alac.answer: No; the law is incomplete and fixes no sufficient standard to guide the agency.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution vests legislative power in Congress. In ABAKADA Guro Party List v. Purisima, G.R. No. 166715, August 14, 2008, the Supreme Court reiterated that a delegation of legislative power is valid only if the law is complete in itself, setting forth the policy to be executed, and fixes a standard that limits the delegate's authority.
alac.application: Here, the law gives the agency unlimited discretion with no policy or standard.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the law is an undue delegation of legislative power and is void.

cite: ABAKADA Guro Party List v. Purisima, G.R. No. 166715, August 14, 2008; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 1

q: A valid exercise of police power requires:
choices: A lawful subject (public interest) and lawful means (reasonably necessary and not unduly oppressive)
hints: Regulation vs. taking.
The most pervasive of the inherent powers.
why: Police power is the power to enact laws to promote public health, safety, morals and general welfare; the tests are lawful subject (the interests of the public generally require it) and lawful means (the means are reasonably necessary and not unduly oppressive). No compensation is due for property regulated, as opposed to property taken for public use.

q: A city ordinance requires all bars to close at 2:00 AM to reduce late-night crime. A bar owner says the ordinance takes his property without compensation. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No; the ordinance is a valid exercise of police power, which regulates property without the need for compensation.
alac.basis: Police power is the inherent power of the State to regulate liberty and property to promote the general welfare. Its exercise is valid when the interests of the public generally require it (lawful subject) and the means are reasonably necessary to accomplish the purpose and not unduly oppressive (lawful means). Mere regulation of property under police power does not require just compensation.
alac.application: Here, reducing late-night crime is a public interest, and limiting closing hours is a reasonable means that does not take the bar itself.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the ordinance is valid and no compensation is due.

q: The constitutional limitations on eminent domain are:
choices: Public use, just compensation and due process
Approval by the courts in advance
hints: Public use is broadly construed.
Taking may occur without transfer of title.
why: Art. III, Sec. 9: private property may be taken only for public use and upon just compensation, with due process; public use now means public advantage or benefit; 'taking' includes depriving the owner of the ordinary use of the property. See also RA 10752 as amended by RA 12289 for infrastructure projects.

q: The government built a dam that permanently flooded part of a farmer's land, without filing any case or paying him. Is there a taking?

alac.answer: Yes; permanently depriving the owner of the use of his land is a taking, for which just compensation must be paid.
alac.basis: Article III, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution provides that private property shall not be taken for public use without just compensation. Under jurisprudence, there is a taking when the owner is deprived of the ordinary use of his property, even without formal expropriation or transfer of title.
alac.application: Here, the flooding permanently deprived the farmer of the use of part of his land for a public project.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the farmer is entitled to just compensation, and may sue to recover it.

q: Under Article VI, Section 28(1), the rule of taxation shall be:
choices: Uniform and equitable, with Congress evolving a progressive system of taxation
hints: Uniformity allows reasonable classification.
Revenue bills originate in the House.
why: Taxation is the inherent power to raise revenue; constitutional limits include uniformity and equity, progressivity, due process, equal protection, exemptions of religious and charitable property (Sec. 28(3)), and the requirement that revenue bills originate in the House (Sec. 24).

q: A law imposes a higher tax on cigarettes than on other goods. A cigarette maker argues this violates uniformity. Is he correct?

alac.answer: No; uniformity allows reasonable classification, and all cigarettes of the same class are taxed alike.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 28(1) of the 1987 Constitution provides that the rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable, and that Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. Uniformity means that all taxable articles of the same class are taxed at the same rate; it does not prohibit reasonable classification based on substantial distinctions.
alac.application: Here, cigarettes form a distinct class, and the tax applies equally to all of them.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the tax is valid.

q: Under Article II, Section 3, which is supreme over the military at all times?
hints: The President is Commander-in-Chief: civilian supremacy.
Most Art. II policies need laws to be enforced.
why: Art. II (Declaration of Principles and State Policies): democratic and republican State; renunciation of war; civilian supremacy; separation of Church and State; independent foreign policy; freedom from nuclear weapons; family, youth, women, labor, environment, health, local autonomy, honest public service. Most are not self-executing, but they guide interpretation.

q: A military general announced that the armed forces will no longer follow the President's orders until certain reforms are made. Which constitutional principle does this violate?

alac.answer: It violates the principle that civilian authority is, at all times, supreme over the military.
alac.basis: Article II, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution provides that civilian authority is, at all times, supreme over the military, and that the Armed Forces of the Philippines is the protector of the people and the State. Under Article VII, Section 18, the President, a civilian, is the Commander-in-Chief of all armed forces.
alac.application: Here, the general claims authority to disobey the civilian Commander-in-Chief.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, his announcement violates civilian supremacy, and he may be disciplined under military law.

keyPoints: Declaration of principles and state policies (Art. II)

q: Under Article I of the Constitution, the national territory includes:
choices: The Philippine archipelago with all its islands and waters, other territories over which the Philippines has sovereignty or jurisdiction, and its terrestrial, fluvial and aerial domains
hints: Waters between the islands are internal waters.
Includes airspace and seabed.
why: Art. I: the archipelago with its islands and waters, other territories under Philippine sovereignty or jurisdiction, the terrestrial, fluvial and aerial domains, including the territorial sea, seabed, subsoil, insular shelves and submarine areas; the waters around, between and connecting the islands are internal waters (archipelagic doctrine).

q: A foreign vessel sailed through the waters between two Philippine islands, claiming they are high seas. Under the Constitution, how are those waters classified?

alac.answer: They are internal waters of the Philippines, regardless of their breadth and dimensions.
alac.basis: Article I of the 1987 Constitution provides that the national territory comprises the Philippine archipelago, with all the islands and waters embraced therein, and that the waters around, between, and connecting the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of the internal waters of the Philippines.
alac.application: Here, the vessel sailed in waters between Philippine islands.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the waters are internal waters, not high seas, subject to the rights of passage recognized under UNCLOS (archipelagic sea lanes).

q: Under Article IV, Section 1, which of the following is a Filipino citizen?
choices: A person born in the Philippines of foreign parents only
A person whose father or mother is a citizen of the Philippines
A foreigner who has lived here for five years
A person married to a Filipino, automatically
hints: Jus sanguinis applies.
Marriage does not by itself confer citizenship.
why: Art. IV, Sec. 1: citizens are (1) citizens at the adoption of the 1987 Constitution; (2) those whose fathers or mothers are citizens (jus sanguinis); (3) those born before January 17, 1973 of Filipino mothers who elect citizenship upon majority; (4) naturalized citizens. The Philippines follows jus sanguinis, not jus soli.

q: A child was born in Japan to a Filipino mother and a Japanese father. Is the child a Filipino citizen?

alac.answer: Yes; the child's mother is a Filipino citizen.
alac.basis: Article IV, Section 1(2) of the 1987 Constitution provides that those whose fathers or mothers are citizens of the Philippines are citizens of the Philippines. The Philippines follows the principle of jus sanguinis, under which citizenship follows that of the parents, regardless of the place of birth.
alac.application: Here, the child's mother is Filipino; the place of birth does not matter.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the child is a Filipino citizen (and may also be a Japanese citizen under Japanese law).

keyPoints: Who are Filipino citizens (Art. IV, Sec. 1)
Place of birth is not decisive

q: Under the Constitution, a foreigner may become a Filipino citizen by:
choices: Naturalization in accordance with law (judicial under CA 473, administrative under RA 9139, or legislative)
hints: Naturalization is strictly construed.
Three modes: judicial, administrative, legislative.
why: Acquisition of citizenship other than by birth is by naturalization: judicial (CA 473, as amended), administrative (RA 9139, for those born and residing in the Philippines), or direct legislative act; naturalization laws are strictly construed against the applicant.

q: A foreigner born and raised in the Philippines, who has lived here all her life, wants to become a Filipino. Which naturalization laws may she use?

alac.answer: She may apply for administrative naturalization under RA 9139, or judicial naturalization under CA 473, if she meets the qualifications.
alac.basis: Article IV, Section 1(4) of the 1987 Constitution provides that those who are naturalized in accordance with law are citizens of the Philippines. The laws provide for judicial naturalization under Commonwealth Act No. 473, as amended, and administrative naturalization under RA 9139 for aliens born and residing in the Philippines; Congress may also naturalize by a special law.
alac.application: Here, she was born and has always resided in the Philippines.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she may use the administrative route under RA 9139, which is simpler, or the judicial route.

q: A natural-born citizen is one who:
choices: Was naturalized at a young age
Is a citizen from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect citizenship (including those who elect citizenship under Sec. 1(3))
Has lived here for ten years
hints: Election under Sec. 1(3) counts as natural-born.
Naturalized citizens are not natural-born.
why: Art. IV, Sec. 2: natural-born citizens are citizens from birth without needing any act; those who elect citizenship under Sec. 1(3) are deemed natural-born. Natural-born citizenship is required for the President, Vice-President, Members of Congress, Justices, and heads of constitutional commissions.

q: A naturalized Filipino citizen wants to run for Senator. May he?

alac.answer: No; a Senator must be a natural-born citizen, and a naturalized citizen is not one.
alac.basis: Article IV, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution defines natural-born citizens as those who are citizens of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their Philippine citizenship. Article VI, Section 3 requires a Senator to be a natural-born citizen.
alac.application: Here, the candidate had to undergo naturalization to become a citizen.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is not qualified to be a Senator.

q: Under RA 9225, a natural-born Filipino who became a foreign citizen by naturalization may reacquire Philippine citizenship by:
choices: Living in the Philippines for one year
Taking the oath of allegiance to the Republic
hints: Oath of allegiance reacquires citizenship.
Renunciation is needed to run for office.
why: Art. IV, Sec. 3 leaves loss and reacquisition to law. RA 9225: natural-born Filipinos who lost citizenship by foreign naturalization reacquire it by taking the oath of allegiance; to run for elective office they must also make a personal and sworn renunciation of foreign citizenship.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. IV, Sec. 3; Citizenship Retention and Re-acquisition Act of 2003 (RA 9225)

q: A natural-born Filipino became a U.S. citizen, then took the oath of allegiance under RA 9225, and now wants to run for mayor. What more must she do?

alac.answer: She must make a personal and sworn renunciation of her U.S. citizenship before filing her certificate of candidacy.
alac.basis: Article IV, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution provides that Philippine citizenship may be lost or reacquired in the manner provided by law. Under RA 9225, natural-born citizens who lost their citizenship by naturalization abroad reacquire it by taking the oath of allegiance, and those seeking elective public office must also make a personal and sworn renunciation of any foreign citizenship.
alac.application: Here, she has reacquired citizenship by her oath but has not renounced her U.S. citizenship.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she must execute the sworn renunciation to qualify as a candidate.

keyPoints: Loss and reacquisition by law (Art. IV, Sec. 3)
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. IV, Sec. 3; Citizenship Retention and Re-acquisition Act of 2003 (RA 9225)

q: Under Mercado v. Manzano, dual citizenship differs from dual allegiance in that dual citizenship:
choices: Arises involuntarily from the concurrent application of different laws, while dual allegiance results from a person's positive act
Requires an oath to two countries
Is the same as dual allegiance
hints: Dual citizenship is not prohibited by the Constitution.
Dual allegiance is the evil addressed.
why: Art. IV, Sec. 5 condemns dual allegiance, not dual citizenship. Mercado v. Manzano, G.R. No. 135083, May 26, 1999: dual citizenship is involuntary (e.g., birth in a jus soli country to Filipino parents); dual allegiance is a person's simultaneous owing of loyalty to two States; for candidates, filing a certificate of candidacy with a declaration of allegiance was held an election of Philippine citizenship.
cite: Mercado v. Manzano, G.R. No. 135083, May 26, 1999; 1987 Constitution, Art. IV, Sec. 5

q: A candidate was born in the U.S. to Filipino parents, making him a citizen of both countries. His opponent says he is disqualified because the Constitution prohibits dual citizenship. Is the opponent correct?

alac.answer: No; the Constitution addresses dual allegiance, not dual citizenship that arises involuntarily from birth.
alac.basis: Article IV, Section 5 of the 1987 Constitution provides that dual allegiance of citizens is inimical to the national interest and shall be dealt with by law. In Mercado v. Manzano, G.R. No. 135083, May 26, 1999, the Supreme Court distinguished dual citizenship, which arises from the concurrent application of the laws of two states, from dual allegiance, which results from a positive act of the person.
alac.application: Here, the candidate's dual citizenship arose from his birth, not from any act of his.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, he is not disqualified on that ground, provided he complies with the election laws on candidates with dual citizenship.

cite: Mercado v. Manzano, G.R. No. 135083, May 26, 1999; 1987 Constitution, Art. IV, Sec. 5

q: A Senator must be, among others:
choices: A natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old on election day, able to read and write, a registered voter, and a resident for at least two years
hints: Age is counted on election day.
Two consecutive terms at most.
why: Art. VI: 24 Senators elected at large (Sec. 2); qualifications (Sec. 3); six-year term, no more than two consecutive terms; voluntary renunciation does not interrupt the term (Sec. 4).

q: A candidate for Senator turns 35 two weeks after the election. Is she qualified?

alac.answer: No; she must be at least thirty-five years of age on the day of the election.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution provides that no person shall be a Senator unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines and, on the day of the election, is at least thirty-five years of age, able to read and write, a registered voter, and a resident of the Philippines for not less than two years immediately preceding the day of the election.
alac.application: Here, the candidate is only 34 on election day.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she is not qualified to be a Senator.

keyPoints: Composition of the Senate (Art. VI, Sec. 2)

q: A member of Congress is privileged from arrest while Congress is in session for offenses punishable by:
choices: Not more than six years imprisonment
hints: Speech immunity protects only from being questioned outside Congress.
Congress may still discipline its own members.
why: Art. VI, Sec. 11: privilege from arrest (offenses punishable by not more than six years, while Congress is in session) and speech or debate immunity (not questioned elsewhere for speeches in Congress or its committees); Secs. 12-14: disclosure of financial interests, incompatible and forbidden offices, and other inhibitions.

q: A Congressman, during a privilege speech in session, accused a businessman of corruption. The businessman filed a libel case. Will it prosper?

alac.answer: No; a member cannot be questioned nor held liable in any other place for any speech or debate in Congress or its committees.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that no member of Congress shall be questioned nor be held liable in any other place for any speech or debate in the Congress or in any committee thereof, in addition to the privilege from arrest for offenses punishable by not more than six years imprisonment while Congress is in session.
alac.application: Here, the accusation was made in a privilege speech during the session.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the libel case will not prosper, although the House itself may discipline the member for disorderly behavior.

q: Under Article VI, Section 16(2), a quorum to do business in each House is:
hints: Members abroad may be excluded in counting quorum.
Different votes for different acts.
why: Quorum: a majority of each House (Sec. 16(2)), counted on the basis of members within the coercive jurisdiction of the House; a smaller number may adjourn and compel attendance. Voting majorities vary: e.g., two-thirds to override a veto or declare war (all members voting separately/jointly), majority of all members to revoke martial law (jointly), three-fourths to propose amendments.

q: The Senate has 24 members, one of whom is abroad. Twelve Senators are present. Is there a quorum?

alac.answer: Yes; the Senator abroad is outside the Senate's coercive jurisdiction, so twelve is a majority of the twenty-three Senators who can be compelled to attend.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 16(2) of the 1987 Constitution provides that a majority of each House shall constitute a quorum to do business. Under jurisprudence, the basis for determining a quorum is the number of members within the coercive jurisdiction of the House.
alac.application: Here, 23 Senators are within the Senate's jurisdiction, and 12 is a majority of 23.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, there is a quorum.

q: Under Article VI, Section 16(3), each House may suspend a member for disorderly behavior for not more than:
choices: Sixty days, with the concurrence of two-thirds of all its members
hints: Two-thirds vote to suspend or expel.
Court-ordered preventive suspension is different.
why: Each House may punish members for disorderly behavior and, with two-thirds of all members, suspend (not more than 60 days) or expel; this is distinct from the preventive suspension under the Anti-Graft Law imposed by the Sandiganbayan, which is not a penalty.

q: The House voted, by two-thirds of all its members, to suspend a member for six months for disorderly behavior. Is the suspension valid?

alac.answer: No; a suspension imposed by the House as a penalty cannot exceed sixty days.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 16(3) of the 1987 Constitution allows each House to punish its members for disorderly behavior and, with the concurrence of two-thirds of all its members, suspend or expel a member, and provides that a penalty of suspension, when imposed, shall not exceed sixty days.
alac.application: Here, the House imposed six months.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the suspension is invalid beyond sixty days.

q: Under Article VI, Section 26(1), every bill shall:
choices: Embrace as many subjects as needed
Embrace only one subject, which shall be expressed in its title
hints: The title need not catalogue every detail.
Provisions germane to the subject are allowed.
why: Limitations on legislative power include the one subject-one title rule (Sec. 26(1)), liberally construed (the title need not be a complete index), no ex post facto law or bill of attainder (Art. III, Sec. 22), no irrepealable laws, and rules on appropriations and taxation.

q: A law titled "An Act Regulating Public Utility Vehicles" contains a section increasing the salaries of judges. Is that section valid?

alac.answer: No; it is not germane to the subject expressed in the title.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 26(1) of the 1987 Constitution provides that every bill passed by Congress shall embrace only one subject which shall be expressed in the title thereof. The rule is liberally construed: the title need not mirror every provision, but provisions must be germane to the subject expressed.
alac.application: Here, judges' salaries have no connection with the regulation of public utility vehicles.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the salary provision is void, while the rest of the law may stand.

keyPoints: One subject-one title rule (Art. VI, Sec. 26(1))

q: Under Article VI, Section 26(2), the three-readings requirement may be dispensed with:
choices: When the President certifies the bill's immediate enactment to meet a public calamity or emergency
hints: Presidential certification of urgency is the exception.
No amendments on third reading.
why: Sec. 26(2): three readings on separate days, with printed copies distributed three days before passage, unless the President certifies the bill as urgent to meet a public calamity or emergency; on the third reading, no amendment is allowed and the vote is by yeas and nays.

q: A bill was passed on second and third readings on the same day, without any presidential certification of urgency. Did it validly pass?

alac.answer: No; without a presidential certification of urgency, the bill must pass three readings on separate days.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 26(2) of the 1987 Constitution provides that no bill passed by either House shall become a law unless it has passed three readings on separate days, and printed copies in its final form have been distributed three days before its passage, except when the President certifies to the necessity of its immediate enactment to meet a public calamity or emergency.
alac.application: Here, the second and third readings were held the same day with no certification.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the bill did not validly pass.

keyPoints: Three readings on separate days (Art. VI, Sec. 26(2))

q: If the President does not act on a bill within thirty days from receipt, the bill:
choices: Becomes a law as if he had signed it
hints: No pocket veto in the Philippines.
Item veto only for appropriation, revenue and tariff bills.
why: Art. VI, Sec. 27: the President may sign or veto a bill (communicating the veto within 30 days to the House of origin); otherwise it becomes law as if signed; item veto applies only to appropriation, revenue and tariff bills; Congress overrides by two-thirds of all members of each House.

q: The President vetoed one provision of a general law on traffic safety while approving the rest. Is the partial veto valid?

alac.answer: No; the item veto applies only to appropriation, revenue and tariff bills; a general law must be approved or vetoed as a whole.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 27 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the President shall communicate his veto of any bill to the House where it originated within thirty days after the date of receipt, otherwise it shall become a law as if he had signed it; Section 27(2) gives the President the power to veto any particular item or items only in an appropriation, revenue, or tariff bill.
alac.application: Here, the traffic safety law is not an appropriation, revenue or tariff bill.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the partial veto is invalid, and the President must approve or veto the bill as a whole.

keyPoints: Veto and lapse into law (Art. VI, Sec. 27)
Item veto limited to appropriation, revenue, tariff bills

q: Under Article VI, Section 29(1), money may be paid out of the Treasury only:
choices: In pursuance of an appropriation made by law
hints: Transfers only to augment items from savings.
No riders in the budget.
why: The power of the purse: no money out of the Treasury without an appropriation by law (Sec. 29(1)); limits on appropriations (Secs. 25 and 29): no increase of the President's budget, no riders, no transfer of appropriations except augmentation of savings by specified officials (Sec. 25(5)), and no public money for religious purposes (Sec. 29(2)).

q: A department secretary used savings from her department's budget to fund a project of another department that has no item in the budget. Is this valid?

alac.answer: No; transfers are allowed only to augment existing items in one's own branch, and no money may be spent without an appropriation for it.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 29(1) of the 1987 Constitution provides that no money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law. Section 25(5) allows only the President, the Senate President, the Speaker, the Chief Justice and the heads of Constitutional Commissions to augment items in the general appropriations law for their respective offices from savings in their other appropriations.
alac.application: Here, the secretary funded a project of another department with no existing item.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the disbursement is unconstitutional.

q: The requisites of a valid legislative inquiry under Article VI, Section 21 include:
choices: It must be in aid of legislation, in accordance with duly published rules, and respect the rights of persons appearing
It must be approved by the President
It may be conducted only by the full House
hints: Rules must be published.
Executive privilege must be claimed specifically.
why: Art. VI, Sec. 21: inquiries in aid of legislation, per duly published rules, respecting the rights of persons appearing; attendance is compulsory (contempt power). Senate v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006: department heads may not be barred by the President from inquiries except on a valid claim of executive privilege; question hour (Sec. 22) appearance is discretionary.
cite: Senate of the Philippines v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 21

q: The President issued an order requiring all executive officials to get her consent before appearing in any Senate inquiry in aid of legislation. Is the order valid?

alac.answer: Not as a blanket rule; officials may be excused only upon a valid and specific claim of executive privilege.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 21 of the 1987 Constitution allows each House or its committees to conduct inquiries in aid of legislation in accordance with its duly published rules of procedure, respecting the rights of persons appearing. In Senate of the Philippines v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006, the Supreme Court held that the President may not prevent executive officials from appearing in such inquiries except through a valid claim of executive privilege, and invalidated the provision requiring prior consent for that purpose.
alac.application: Here, the order bars appearances without any specific claim of privilege.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the order is invalid insofar as it applies to inquiries in aid of legislation.

keyPoints: Power of legislative inquiry (Art. VI, Sec. 21)
cite: Senate of the Philippines v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 21

q: In the question hour under Article VI, Section 22, the appearance of department heads is:
choices: Discretionary, upon their own initiative with the President's consent, or upon the request of either House
hints: Question hour: oversight, voluntary.
Inquiry: legislation, compulsory.
why: Art. VI, Sec. 22: question hour relates to the oversight function; appearance of department heads is discretionary and may be prevented by the President; contrast with Sec. 21 inquiries in aid of legislation, where attendance is compulsory (Senate v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006).
cite: Senate of the Philippines v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 22

q: The House invited a Cabinet secretary to appear in its question hour. The President told him not to attend. May the House cite him in contempt?

alac.answer: No; appearance in the question hour is discretionary, and the President may withhold consent.
alac.basis: Article VI, Section 22 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the heads of departments may upon their own initiative, with the consent of the President, or upon the request of either House, appear before and be heard by such House on any matter pertaining to their departments. In Senate of the Philippines v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006, the Supreme Court held that appearance in the question hour, unlike in an inquiry in aid of legislation, is not mandatory.
alac.application: Here, the invitation was for the question hour, and the President withheld consent.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the secretary cannot be cited in contempt for not appearing.

keyPoints: Contrast with inquiries in aid of legislation
cite: Senate of the Philippines v. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006; 1987 Constitution, Art. VI, Sec. 22

q: Under Francisco v. House of Representatives, impeachment proceedings are "initiated" when:
choices: The Senate convenes as a court
A verified complaint is filed and referred to the House Committee on Justice
The House votes on the articles
hints: One-year bar counts from initiation.
One-third of the House to impeach; two-thirds of the Senate to convict.
why: Art. XI: impeachable officers (President, Vice-President, Justices of the SC, members of Constitutional Commissions, Ombudsman); grounds (culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, betrayal of public trust); the House initiates (one-third vote to impeach), the Senate tries (two-thirds to convict); one-year bar (Sec. 3(5)). Francisco v. House, G.R. No. 160261, November 10, 2003: initiation = filing and referral to the Committee on Justice.
cite: Francisco v. House of Representatives, G.R. No. 160261, November 10, 2003; 1987 Constitution, Art. XI, Secs. 2 and 3

q: In March, an impeachment complaint against the Ombudsman was filed and referred to the House Committee on Justice, which dismissed it. In August of the same year, a second complaint against her was filed. May it proceed?

alac.answer: No; the second complaint is barred because proceedings were already initiated against the same official within one year.
alac.basis: Article XI, Section 3(5) of the 1987 Constitution provides that no impeachment proceedings shall be initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year. In Francisco v. House of Representatives, G.R. No. 160261, November 10, 2003, the Supreme Court held that impeachment proceedings are initiated by the filing of a verified complaint and its referral to the House Committee on Justice.
alac.application: Here, the first complaint was filed and referred in March, so proceedings were initiated then; the August complaint is within one year.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the second complaint cannot proceed until the one-year period lapses.

cite: Francisco v. House of Representatives, G.R. No. 160261, November 10, 2003; 1987 Constitution, Art. XI, Secs. 2 and 3
